statement: Sofia read a third of her book on Monday and a quarter of the whole book on Tuesday. On Tuesday she read 4 pages fewer than on Monday. How many pages does the book have?

choices.misconception: I found the number of pages she read on Monday instead of the number in the whole book.
I found the pages she still has to read after Tuesday instead of the whole book.
I found that one twelfth of the book is 4 pages, but then I worked out the 7 twelfths she read over both days instead of the whole book.
I found the number of pages she read on Tuesday instead of the number in the whole book.

hints: Split the book into equal parts that both a third and a quarter fit.
Use 12 equal parts: a third of the book is 4 of those parts and a quarter is 3 of them. Compare Monday with Tuesday in parts.
Monday was 4 parts and Tuesday was 3 parts, so the 4 pages are exactly 1 part.

solutions.reliable: Cut the book into 12 equal parts. A third of the book is 4 parts and a quarter is 3 parts. Monday's reading was 1 part more than Tuesday's, and that difference is 4 pages, so 1 part is 4 pages. The whole book is 12 parts, which is 12 x 4 = 48 pages. Check: a third of 48 is 16, a quarter of 48 is 12, and 16 - 12 = 4. The transferable idea: to compare two fractions of the same whole, cut the whole into equal parts that both fractions fit, then find what one part is worth.

whyOnTest: Fractions of a quantity: comparing a third and a quarter of the same book means finding equal parts that both fit, which is what makes this a 5-point problem.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
